content.title: About
content.content: Eel is a marine fish of the family Anguillidae, found in rivers, lakes and coastal seas of the Northern Hemisphere. Its flesh is dark‑red, firm, and has a slightly sweet flavor. Eel is commonly used in sushi, grilling, smoking, and traditional dishes such as Japanese “unagi.”

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eels can migrate between fresh and salt water, undertaking a spawning migration known as the “silver eel” phase.
In Japan, eel is a delicacy often served as grilled “unagi” with a sweet soy‑based sauce.
There are over 800 eel species, but the European (Anguilla anguilla) and American (Anguilla rostrata) eels are most commonly used in cuisine.
Eels produce a mucus layer that protects their skin from parasites and infections.
In some cultures, eel symbolizes longevity and strength.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Eel meat contains EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Eel provides a complete set of essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eel is a good source of B12, B1 and B6, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals aid hemoglobin formation and immune support.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked eel may contain parasites; it should be cooked to at least 70 °C.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Marinated or smoked eel can be high in salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to seafood may react to eel.

items.title: Heavy metals
items.content: Eels from polluted waters can accumulate cadmium and mercury; purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eel can be grilled, baked, steamed, or smoked. In Japan it is often served as “unagi” grilled with a sweet soy glaze. The flesh is sliced thin for sushi, added to salads, or used in stews. Before cooking, remove the skin and innards.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh eel should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and used within 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it at –18 °C in an airtight bag. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature.
